doc.title: Jim Hall — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: Well, it brings me to someone I want to ask you about.
Okay, all right.

I wanted to ask you a little bit about Miles Davis in his later years. Because my recollection is, in my younger days, is that you were interested in what he was doing. You actually went to hear him someplace, and I was astounded by that. So…
That I, that I was interested, you mean?
Mm-hmm.
Yeah.
‘Cause he was way out there at that point. It wasn’t…
Really?
Yeah, it wasn’t like Sketches of Spain or those era. It was, it was sort of almost rock fusion at that point.
Oh, oh.
And I didn’t know that would interest you.
I don’t remember, either. That… I’d forgotten that he kinda went in that… I think… didn’t Metheny work with him, or one of those guys, for a while?
Maybe.
Yeah.

What I’m seeing, in retrospect, and what I’m hearing from you is your interest and your intrigue in the possibilities and things that haven’t been done yet, and I’m wondering if that’s what you were seeing in…
In Miles?
…him and his exploration.

Well, I would imagine, and I am imagining, that I probably wouldn’t have been too thrilled at hearing that music. But I always admired Miles Davis and still do. And he, he, you know, he came along at a fascinating time and he had worked with Charlie Parker and everything and… I loved his voice, too—a cute, kinda salty sounding voice. It’s also interesting… literally, that I’ve talked to Brian Camelio about that and Brian actually liked Chet Baker’s playing better than Miles’. And I can understand that. It is… Miles had kind of a… an attitude or something. His, his presence was really strong. And then Miles had the courage in those days to call Bill Evans and get Bill involved. So Miles was searching constantly, as well, I think. And he had that great group that I told you we played opposite. We had… what was Cannonball’s real name? Julian or…?
Mm-hmm.

And then he had John Coltrane, Paul Chambers, Philly Joe Jones and Bill Evans. And that, that was fairly avant-garde ‘cause he had this waspy piano player who was really tuned in and sensitive and everything so… I really admired that part of Miles, where he was willing to go ahead and take chances on other things. Again, I didn’t… wasn’t always thrilled with the, the mud he stepped into there, (laughs) but he was at least trying so… And then, and again, that’s the fascination, I assume, with getting up every morning and then picking up the guitar every day. And I told you I, I did it to one of these ‘cause I tune them randomly occasionally, just to keep my interest, you know.
